# sysutils_kernel_module (Resource)

Loads a kernel module with `modprobe(8)` and, optionally, configures it to be loaded at boot through `/etc/modules-load.d/<name>.conf` and `/etc/modprobe.d/<name>.conf`. Whether the module is loaded is read from `/proc/modules`. On destroy the configuration files are removed and the module is unloaded with `modprobe -r`. Requires root privileges.

It covers the same ground as Ansible's `modprobe` module with `persistent: present`.

## Example Usage

```terraform
# Kubernetes nodes need bridged traffic to pass through iptables.
resource "sysutils_kernel_module" "br_netfilter" {
  name = "br_netfilter"
}

resource "sysutils_sysctl" "bridge_nf_call_iptables" {
  # The parameter only exists once the module is loaded.
  name  = "net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables"
  value = "1"

  depends_on = [sysutils_kernel_module.br_netfilter]
}

# A module with parameters. They are passed to modprobe and written to
# /etc/modprobe.d/dummy.conf.
resource "sysutils_kernel_module" "dummy" {
  name = "dummy"
  parameters = {
    numdummies = "2"
  }
}

# Loaded now, but not at boot.
resource "sysutils_kernel_module" "wireguard" {
  name    = "wireguard"
  persist = false
}
```

<!-- schema generated by tfplugindocs -->
## Schema

### Required

- `name` (String) Name of the module, such as `"br_netfilter"`. 1 to 55 letters, digits, `_` or `-`, starting with a letter or digit; `-` and `_` are interchangeable, as in `modprobe`. Also names the configuration files. Changing this forces a new resource.

### Optional

- `parameters` (Map of String) Module parameters, such as `{ numdummies = "2" }`, passed to `modprobe` as `name=value` and, with `persist`, written to `/etc/modprobe.d/<name>.conf` as an `options` line. Parameters only take effect when the module is loaded, so changing them on a loaded module unloads and reloads it, which fails while the module is in use. Names consist of letters, digits, `_`, `-` and `.`; values of letters, digits and `_.,:/+=@%-`, without white space or quotes.
- `persist` (Boolean) Whether the module is loaded at boot. If `true`, `/etc/modules-load.d/<name>.conf` lists the module and, if `parameters` is not empty, `/etc/modprobe.d/<name>.conf` sets its parameters; the parameters then also apply when the module is loaded by other means, such as automatically for a device. If `false`, both files are removed. Defaults to `true`.

### Read-Only

- `id` (String) Resource identifier (equal to `name`).

## Behavior

### Create

1. The provider refuses to create the resource if `/etc/modules-load.d/<name>.conf` or `/etc/modprobe.d/<name>.conf` exists and was not written by the resource, for example because a package installed it. Destroying the resource would remove the file, so import the module instead, or remove the file.
2. If `persist` is `true`, `/etc/modules-load.d/<name>.conf` is written with the module name and, if `parameters` is not empty, `/etc/modprobe.d/<name>.conf` with the line `options <name> <parameter>=<value> ...`. If `persist` is `false`, both files are removed.
3. The module is loaded with `modprobe -- <name> <parameter>=<value> ...`.
4. The provider checks that `/proc/modules` lists the module.

The configuration is written first because `modprobe` also applies the options in `/etc/modprobe.d`, which must not contain stale parameters. If loading fails, both files are restored to what they were, so that a module or parameters the kernel rejects are not loaded again at every boot.

If the module is already loaded, for example because it was loaded automatically for a device, it is not reloaded, since unloading it could take down a device or a network interface. Its `parameters` then only take effect the next time it is loaded, and the apply shows a warning saying so.

### Update

- Changed `parameters` on a loaded module unload it with `modprobe -r`, rewrite the configuration and load it again with the new parameters. If unloading fails, because the module is in use, the apply fails without any change. If loading fails, the previous configuration is restored and the module is loaded again with the previous parameters.
- `persist = false` removes both configuration files and `persist = true` writes them. The module is not reloaded.
- Changing `name` replaces the resource.

### Destroy

Both configuration files are removed, then the module is unloaded with `modprobe -r -- <name>`, which also unloads the modules it depended on if nothing else uses them. If the module cannot be unloaded, because it is in use, destroy only warns: the module is no longer loaded at boot, and stays loaded until it is unloaded manually or the system reboots.

## Validation

- `name` must match `^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9_-]{0,54}$`: 1 to 55 characters, the kernel's limit. It can therefore neither be taken for a `modprobe` option nor leave the configuration directories when used as a file name.
- Parameter names must match `^[A-Za-z0-9_][A-Za-z0-9_.-]{0,127}$`, and values `^[A-Za-z0-9_.,:/+=@%-]*$`, at most 1024 characters. Values with white space, quotes or `#` would need quoting that `modprobe.d` files and the kernel's parameter parser treat differently, so they are rejected at plan time.

## Drift Detection

On refresh the provider reads `/proc/modules` and the two configuration files:

- If `/proc/modules` does not list the module, for example because it was unloaded with `modprobe -r`, the resource is removed from the state, and the next apply loads it again. `-` and `_` in `name` are alike, as `/proc/modules` always shows `_`.
- `persist` is `true` only if both files are exactly as the resource writes them for the current `parameters`. If a file was edited, removed or added, the plan shows `persist` changing to `true`, and the next apply rewrites the files without reloading the module.
- The parameters of the loaded module are not read back: many are not visible in `/sys/module/<name>/parameters`, and those that are use their own formats, such as `Y` for `1`. `parameters` therefore reflects what was last applied.

## Import

A loaded module can be imported by name:

```shell
# By name. The module must be loaded; parameters come from
# /etc/modprobe.d/<name>.conf, if it sets any.
terraform import sysutils_kernel_module.br_netfilter br_netfilter
```

`parameters` are read from the `options` lines for the module in `/etc/modprobe.d/<name>.conf`, if there are any. `persist` is `true` only if both configuration files are in the resource's own format; otherwise the first apply rewrites them. The import fails if the module is not loaded.

## Caveats

- The resource requires root with `CAP_SYS_MODULE`. Containers usually lack it, and cannot load modules for the host's kernel even with it unless its module tree is mounted.
- Modules built into the kernel are not listed in `/proc/modules` and cannot be managed; the apply fails with an error that says so.
- `modprobe` is limited to 2 minutes per call, so a module that waits for missing firmware or hardware cannot hang the apply forever.
- `install` and `remove` commands, blacklists and aliases in `/etc/modprobe.d` apply as they do at boot. A blacklisted module can still be loaded by name.
- The resource cannot be used with the provider's `root_dir` argument: it loads modules into the running kernel and writes the configuration of the host, so it refuses to plan when `root_dir` is set. Use a separate provider configuration without `root_dir` for it.
- `/etc/modules-load.d` is read by `systemd-modules-load.service`. Distributions without systemd may need `/etc/modules` instead, which the resource does not manage.
